indicators.title: Grain in storage
indicators.question: Is there more or less grain in the country's elevators and ports than usual for this time of year?
indicators.definition: Wheat, canola and other grains held in licensed grain elevators across the Prairies and at port terminals, as reported each week by the Canadian Grain Commission.
indicators.how_calculated: We add up all grain in storage at the end of the latest week and compare the total with the same week in each of the past five crop years.
indicators.does_not_show: Grain still on farms, which is most of Canada's grain, and food further along the chain. A high number can mean a comfortable reserve, or grain that cannot move. Read it alongside grain shipped through ports.

headline.text: Grain elevators and port terminals held 7.25 million tonnes of grain in the week ending 4 October 2026. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past five years. It is about 2% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same week in each of the past 5 crop years (at least 3 needed). A crop year runs from August to July.

indicators.title: Grain shipped through ports
indicators.question: Is grain leaving Canada's ports at a normal pace?
indicators.definition: Grain and oilseeds shipped abroad from port terminals in Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Thunder Bay, the St. Lawrence and elsewhere, reported each week by the Canadian Grain Commission.
indicators.how_calculated: We add up the latest four weeks, because ships arrive unevenly, and compare the total with the same four weeks in each of the past five crop years.
indicators.does_not_show: Why the pace changed. A slowdown can come from rail or port problems, weather, a smaller harvest or weaker sales. Grain sent to the United States by rail or truck is not included.

headline.text: Ports shipped 3.21 million tonnes of grain abroad in the four weeks to 4 October 2026. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past five years. It is about 4% above the typical level.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same week in each of the past 5 crop years (at least 3 needed). A crop year runs from August to July.

indicators.title: Fresh fruit and vegetable prices
indicators.question: Are fresh fruit and vegetable prices unusual for this time of year?
indicators.unit: Canadian dollars per box or bag
indicators.definition: Daily wholesale prices at the Toronto wholesale market for 12 fruits and vegetables, from Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada. Each product is always the same variety, grade, origin and box size, so its price can be compared over time.
indicators.how_calculated: For each product we take the average price in the latest week and compare it with the same week in up to 5 past years. Past prices are first converted to October 2026's dollars using the Consumer Price Index, so inflation alone does not make today's prices look high. A product is flagged only if this week's price is above or below every past year.
indicators.does_not_show: What shoppers pay in stores, prices in other cities, or why a price changed. Weather where the food is grown, the exchange rate, quality and the timing of harvests all move wholesale prices.

headline.text: We follow 12 fresh fruits and vegetables at the Toronto wholesale market. In the latest week, two cost more and two cost less than at this time of year in any recent year, after allowing for inflation. Four are in their normal range, and for four we do not have enough past data.

items.label: Iceberg lettuce, field, imported from the United States
items.text: $56.50–$68.00 per Ctn 30 Cello on 19 November 2026. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past three years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 15% below the typical level.

items.label: Strawberries, field, imported from the United States
items.text: $59.00–$64.00 per Ctn 8X1 lbs on 19 November 2026. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past four years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 25% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

items.label: Broccoli, green bunched, imported from the United States
items.text: $48.00 per Ctn 18 Bchd on 19 November 2026. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past three years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 9% above the typical level.

items.label: Navel oranges, imported from California
items.text: $31.00–$45.00 per Ctn 72 on 19 November 2026. We do not have enough past years of comparable data to say whether this is normal.

items.label: Avocados, imported from Mexico
items.text: $37.00–$50.00 per Ctn 48 on 19 November 2026. That is lower than at this time of year in any of the past four years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 33% below the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

items.label: Bananas, imported from Costa Rica
items.text: $25.93 per Ctn 40 lbs on 19 November 2026. We do not have enough past years of comparable data to say whether this is normal.

items.label: Tomatoes on the vine, Ontario greenhouse
items.text: $22.00 per Ctn 11 lbs on 19 November 2026. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past three years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 14% above the typical level.

items.label: Red peppers, Ontario greenhouse
items.text: $36.00 per Ctn 11 lbs Xlge on 19 November 2026. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past four years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 19% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

items.label: Carrots, jumbo, Ontario
items.text: $15.00–$17.50 per Ctn 50 lbs Jbo on 19 November 2026. That is lower than at this time of year in any of the past four years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 27% below the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

items.label: Red potatoes, Canada
items.text: $3.90 per Bag 10 lbs on 19 November 2026. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past three years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 2% below the typical level.

items.label: Green cabbage, Canada
items.text: $23.00–$25.00 per Ctn 50 lbs on 19 November 2026. We do not have enough past years of comparable data to say whether this is normal.

items.label: McIntosh apples, Canada
items.text: $46.50 per Ctn 38 lbs 100 on 19 November 2026. We do not have enough past years of comparable data to say whether this is normal.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same week in up to 5 past years, in today's dollars (at least 3 years needed).

indicators.title: Grocery prices compared with wages
indicators.question: Are grocery prices rising faster than what people earn?
indicators.definition: How much grocery prices changed over 12 months (Statistics Canada's Consumer Price Index for food bought in stores), set against how much the average hourly wage changed over the same 12 months (Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey).
indicators.how_calculated: For each month we compare prices and wages with the same month a year earlier. The gap is the difference between the two changes, in percentage points.
indicators.does_not_show: Who is struggling. National averages hide people without wages, such as pensioners and people on income support, differences between regions, and households that spend a larger share of their income on food.

headline.text: In October 2026, grocery prices were 2.0% higher than a year earlier, and average hourly wages were 2.2% higher. Wages have risen faster than grocery prices for two months in a row.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month one year earlier.

indicators.title: Food recalls
indicators.question: Is the Canadian Food Inspection Agency recalling more food than usual?
indicators.definition: Food recall and safety notices from the Canadian Food Inspection Agency, published on the Government of Canada's recalls website.
indicators.how_calculated: We count notices in the latest 30 days and compare the count with the same 30 days in each of the past 5 years.
indicators.does_not_show: How much food was affected. Most recalls cover one brand or one batch and do not affect supply. The data give the date a notice was last updated, not first issued, so counts are approximate.

headline.text: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency issued 21 food recall notices in the 30 days to 20 November 2026. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past five years. It is about 12% below the typical level.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same 30 days in each of the past 5 years.

indicators.title: Weather warnings
indicators.question: Which weather warnings are in effect, and where?
indicators.definition: Warnings, watches, advisories and special statements from Environment and Climate Change Canada. Alerts of the same type issued at the same time in one province count once.
indicators.how_calculated: We count alerts that have not yet expired. The map on the overview page also checks Environment and Climate Change Canada's service directly each time you open it.
indicators.does_not_show: Whether farms, livestock or transport are actually affected. Alert areas are forecast regions, not farmland.

headline.text: 11 weather alerts were in effect in four provinces or territories when we last checked, including five warnings.

indicators.title: Ships through key sea lanes
indicators.question: Are ships getting through the narrow sea lanes that carry fuel and fertilizer?
indicators.definition: Ships passing through four narrow sea lanes each day: the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea, and the Panama Canal. The International Monetary Fund's PortWatch estimates the counts from ships' tracking signals.
indicators.how_calculated: We take the average number of ships a day over the latest four weeks and compare it with the same four weeks in each of the past five years.
indicators.does_not_show: What the ships carry, or whether cargo found another route. Counts are estimates from tracking signals, which some ships switch off. Recent weeks can be revised.

headline.text: Ships through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 3 a day over the four weeks to 15 November 2026. In the same weeks of the past five years the typical figure was about 86 a day. That is below the range of every one of those years, about 96% below the typical level. Also unusual: Bab el-Mandeb Strait (fewer ships than usual).

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same week in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: Cargo loaded at Canadian ports
indicators.question: Are Canada's main ports loading cargo at a normal pace?
indicators.definition: Estimated tonnes of cargo loaded onto ships each day at Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Montreal, Halifax and Thunder Bay. PortWatch estimates the tonnage from ships' tracking signals and how low they sit in the water.
indicators.how_calculated: We average the latest four weeks and compare that with the same four weeks in each of the past five years.
indicators.does_not_show: What the cargo is. Vancouver and Prince Rupert load grain, potash, coal and containers together. Thunder Bay closes for winter. Use the grain-shipments indicator for grain.

headline.text: Ships loaded an estimated 1.5 million tonnes a week at the Port of Vancouver in the four weeks to 13 November 2026. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past five years. It is about 8% above the typical level. Elsewhere, unusual: Montreal (more than usual).

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same week in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: World fertilizer prices
indicators.question: Is fertilizer getting more expensive on world markets?
indicators.definition: Monthly world prices for phosphate fertilizer (DAP), nitrogen fertilizer (urea), potash and phosphate rock, and the World Bank's index of fertilizer prices, from the World Bank's monthly commodity price data.
indicators.how_calculated: We compare the latest month with the same month in each of the past five years, in US dollars.
indicators.does_not_show: What Canadian farmers pay. That depends on the exchange rate, freight, and when farmers bought. See the farm input price index for prices paid in Canada.

headline.text: In October 2026, the World Bank's fertilizer price index stood at 148 (2010 = 100), 6% higher than a year earlier. Prices: DAP US$803 a tonne; Urea US$420 a tonne. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past five years, in US dollars without adjusting for inflation. It is about 8% below the typical level.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: World food and energy prices
indicators.question: Are world prices for food and fuel unusually high?
indicators.definition: The World Bank's monthly indices of world food and energy prices, with crude oil, wheat and maize prices. Canada sells wheat at world prices and buys fuel and much of its food at world prices.
indicators.how_calculated: We compare the latest month with the same month in each of the past five years, in US dollars.
indicators.does_not_show: Prices in Canadian stores, which follow world prices with a lag of months and also reflect wages, transport, the exchange rate and competition.

headline.text: In October 2026, the World Bank's food price index stood at 122 (2010 = 100), 15% higher than a year earlier. Energy prices were 89% higher than a year earlier. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past five years, in US dollars without adjusting for inflation.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: Diesel prices
indicators.question: Is diesel, which runs tractors, trucks and trains, unusually expensive?
indicators.definition: Average retail price of diesel at self-serve stations in Montréal, Toronto, Regina, Calgary and Vancouver, from Statistics Canada. Statistics Canada does not publish a national average for diesel.
indicators.how_calculated: We average the five cities and compare the latest month with the same month in each of the past five years, in today's dollars.
indicators.does_not_show: Farm fuel, which is often bought in bulk and taxed differently, or the price paid by large trucking firms on contract.

headline.text: Diesel at self-serve pumps averaged 262.9 cents a litre across five cities in October 2026, 71% more than a year earlier. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past five years, after allowing for inflation. It is about 51% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed), in today's dollars.

indicators.title: What farmers pay for inputs
indicators.question: Are the costs of growing food rising?
indicators.definition: Statistics Canada's farm input price index: what Canadian farmers pay for fertilizer, fuel, seed, feed and other inputs. Published every three months.
indicators.how_calculated: We compare the latest quarter with the same quarter in each of the past five years. The index is not adjusted for inflation.
indicators.does_not_show: Farm incomes or crop prices. Higher costs squeeze farmers most when crop prices are falling at the same time.

headline.text: In the quarter starting April 2026, the prices Canadian farmers paid for all inputs stood at 187 on Statistics Canada's index (2020 = 100), 11% higher than a year earlier. Fertilizer alone was 24% higher. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past five years. It is about 20% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same quarter in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: Store prices for everyday foods
indicators.question: Are everyday foods unusually expensive in stores?
indicators.definition: Average monthly shelf prices across Canada for 15 everyday foods, from Statistics Canada's retail price survey.
indicators.how_calculated: For each food we compare the latest month with the same month in each of the past five years, in today's dollars.
indicators.does_not_show: Sale prices, store brands versus name brands, or prices in remote and northern communities, which are often far higher.

headline.text: We follow 15 everyday foods in Canadian stores. In September 2026, two cost more and three cost less than in the same month of any of the past five years, after allowing for inflation. Higher than usual: ground beef, whole chicken.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed), in today's dollars.

indicators.title: Grocery price rises by province
indicators.question: Are grocery prices rising faster in some provinces than others?
indicators.definition: The 12-month change in the Consumer Price Index for food bought in stores, for each province, from Statistics Canada.
indicators.how_calculated: For each province we compare the latest month with the same month a year earlier.
indicators.does_not_show: Price levels (a smaller rise can still leave prices higher), or the territories, which Statistics Canada publishes for capital cities only.

headline.text: In October 2026, grocery prices were up most in Quebec (+3.0% on a year earlier) and least in Prince Edward Island (+0.1%). The national figure was +2.0%.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month one year earlier.

indicators.title: People who struggle to afford food
indicators.question: How many people live in households that cannot reliably afford enough food?
indicators.definition: The share of people living in households that reported food insecurity (worry about running out of food, eating less, or going without because of money) in Statistics Canada's Canadian Income Survey.
indicators.how_calculated: We show the published shares for each survey year. There is no 'unusual' test: the series is too short and annual.
indicators.does_not_show: This year's situation, the territories, or people living on reserves, in institutions or without housing.
indicators.baseline_rule: Shown as published, year by year.

headline.text: In 2024, 24.0% of people in the ten provinces lived in a household that struggled to afford food, up from 16.8% in 2018. Among children it was 30.8%. This survey is published once a year, more than a year after the fact.

items.label: All people living in food-insecure households

indicators.title: Grain and fertilizer moved by rail
indicators.question: Are trains moving grain and fertilizer at a normal pace?
indicators.definition: Tonnes of grain, canola, potash and other fertilizer loaded onto Canadian railways each month, from Statistics Canada.
indicators.how_calculated: We compare the latest month with the same month in each of the past five years.
indicators.does_not_show: Delays within a month, or grain and fertilizer moved by truck. Figures arrive about two months after the month ends.

headline.text: Railways carried 3.8 million tonnes of wheat, other grains and canola in August 2026. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past five years. It is about 80% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: Strikes and lockouts
indicators.question: Are strikes or lockouts likely to stop food or farm inputs from moving?
indicators.definition: The number of strikes and lockouts under way each month, from Employment and Social Development Canada's records as published by Statistics Canada.
indicators.how_calculated: We compare the latest month with the same month in each of the past five years.
indicators.does_not_show: Which employers are involved. A single stoppage at a railway or port can matter more than dozens elsewhere. Figures arrive about three months late; watch the news notices for current disputes.

headline.text: There were 68 strikes and lockouts under way in Canada in August 2026, five of them in transportation. That is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past five years. It is about 24% above the typical level.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: The Canadian dollar
indicators.question: Is a weak Canadian dollar making imported food dearer?
indicators.definition: How many Canadian dollars one US dollar and one Mexican peso cost, as a monthly average of the Bank of Canada's daily rates. Most imported fruit and vegetables come from the United States and Mexico, and fertilizer and fuel are priced in US dollars.
indicators.how_calculated: We compare the latest month's average with the same month in each of the past five years. A higher number means a weaker Canadian dollar.
indicators.does_not_show: How quickly importers pass on changes, which can take months, or the effect of hedging contracts.

headline.text: One US dollar cost $1.42 Canadian on average so far in November 2026, 0.8% more than a year earlier. A weaker Canadian dollar makes imported food and farm inputs dearer. That is higher than at this time of year in any of the past five years. It is about 3% above the typical level. Worth watching. One unusual reading does not mean a crisis.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: Drought on the Prairies
indicators.question: How much Prairie farmland is in drought?
indicators.definition: The share of the farming south of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba in moderate drought or worse (categories D1 to D4) on Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's Canadian Drought Monitor, published monthly.
indicators.how_calculated: We overlay the monitor's drought areas on three boxes covering each province south of 54° north, and measure the share of each box in drought using an equal-area map projection. We compare it with the same month in earlier years.
indicators.does_not_show: Crop yields. Drought late in the season matters less than drought at seeding or flowering. The boxes include some forest, lakes and towns, so the shares are approximate.

headline.text: At the end of October 2026, 37% of southern Alberta, 0% of southern Saskatchewan and 25% of southern Manitoba were in moderate drought or worse. In Alberta, the province with the most drought, that is normal for this time of year: it is within the range of the past three years. It is about 52% below the typical level.

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same month in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).

indicators.title: Drought where imported produce grows
indicators.question: Is drought hitting the US states that grow much of Canada's imported fruit and vegetables?
indicators.definition: The share of California, Arizona, Florida and Washington in moderate drought or worse, from the weekly US Drought Monitor. California: lettuce, strawberries, broccoli, oranges. Arizona: winter lettuce and leafy greens. Florida: winter tomatoes, peppers and citrus. Washington: apples and pears.
indicators.how_calculated: We compare the latest week with the same week in each of the past five years.
indicators.does_not_show: Whether irrigated farms have enough water, which depends on reservoirs and water rights more than on rainfall.

headline.text: In the week of 17 November 2026, 9% of California; 9% of Arizona; 7% of Florida; 59% of Washington was in moderate drought or worse. Unusual for the time of year: Arizona (less drought than in any of the past five years).

indicators.baseline_rule: Compared with the same week in each of the past 5 years (at least 3 needed).
